name: Rafael Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at an electronics plant that builds circuit boards for smart electricity meters and car chargers. I run a pick-and-place line, which is a machine that grabs tiny parts off reels and drops them onto the boards, hundreds a minute, then the boards go through a reflow oven that melts the solder. My job is loading the reels, swapping them when they run out, clearing jams and checking the boards under a microscope. I've been there eighteen months and I still mix up reels sometimes, which the machine catches, luckily, before it builds a hundred wrong boards.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does it feel to you, day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I find it pretty interesting, it's like looking after a very fast, very stupid robot. I'm doing an online course on PLCs in the evenings, those are the little computers that control factory machines, and I ask an AI assistant about it every day. The boring part is the twelve-hour weekend shifts. I live alone with my cat, so I listen to podcasts on the drive in and try not to think about how early it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit surprised, but okay. I'd probably post that people overestimated it in the short run, like they always do with new tech. Then get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be fine for me, I'd just keep doing my PLC course and try to become a process technician. I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was kind of hoping for something more interesting. My investments in tech funds would probably drop, which would sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course, it's about six months left, and apply for the technician opening when it comes up. I'd keep putting about six hundred a month into a mix of funds. I'd keep using AI to study, because it's still useful even if it's not world-changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, like a film that doesn't have a twist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned tech funds. How did a junior operator end up with investments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I started at nineteen in a warehouse and I've always lived cheap. I lost a chunk on crypto at twenty-three, which taught me a lesson, so now it's boring index funds. It's a bit over a year of expenses, plus my car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would agree with you, and who wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our engineer, Priya, would agree, she thinks AI is overhyped for factory floors. My mate Luka on the next line would say I told you so, he thinks it's all nonsense. We have the argument every lunch break.

S0.say: I'd say I'm a bit surprised but okay, and post that people overestimated new tech in the short run as usual. Then he'd get back to work.
S0.think: It'd be fine; he'd keep doing his PLC course and aim for process technician. He'd be slightly disappointed and his tech funds would likely drop.
S0.do: Finishes the six months left on his PLC course and applies for a technician opening. Keeps investing about six hundred a month in funds and keeps using AI to study.
S0.feel: Calm but slightly flat, like a film without a twist.
S0.quote: I lost a chunk on crypto at twenty-three, which taught me a lesson, so now it's boring index funds.
S0.fieldNote: He enjoys technology, calls his machine a very fast, very stupid robot, and would find a plateau mildly disappointing. His cushion comes from frugal living and a lesson learned from crypto losses. His career plan doesn't depend on AI either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to learn. If you learn how the new systems work, you'll be the one they keep. I'd tell people at work to get on the courses early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me, honestly. Loading reels and checking boards is exactly what vision systems and robot arms will take, but setting them up and fixing them needs people like the person I'm trying to become. I'd be one of the first to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course and do a robot programming certificate on top, probably about two thousand of my own money. I'd ask to be put on any automation project at the plant. If they didn't offer one, I'd apply to the integrator companies that install these lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, bit excited. Like the game just got more interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell people to get on courses early. What about people who don't want to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I find hard. Luka's a good operator, better than me, but he won't touch a laptop. I can't make him, and I don't think it's anyone's fault really, it's just how he is. I'd try to drag him along to one class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd spend two thousand of your own money. Is that a big decision for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I think of it like the crypto lesson in reverse, put money into something I can control, which is my own skills. If it works, the technician pay rise pays it back within a year.

S1.say: I'd say it's a good time to learn, because those who understand new systems get kept. He'd urge colleagues onto courses early.
S1.think: Privately he thinks it's good for him: vision systems will take reel loading and board checks, but setup and repair need people like the technician he's becoming. He'd move early.
S1.do: Finishes the PLC course and pays about two thousand for a robot programming certificate. Asks to join automation projects at the plant, or applies to companies that install these lines.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, as if the game got more interesting.
S1.quote: I think of it like the crypto lesson in reverse, put money into something I can control, which is my own skills.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady disruption as an opportunity and would spend his own money to get ahead. He doesn't blame anyone, including colleagues who resist. His caring side shows in wanting to drag Luka to one class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a wild couple of years and everyone needs to pay attention. I'd say governments should get support in place quickly, because a lot of people are going to need it. I wouldn't say it's the end of the world, but I wouldn't say it's fine either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too fast even for me. My whole plan was to be the guy who fixes the robots, and in this one the robots fix themselves pretty quickly. My savings help, but they help for a year or two, not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get hired by one of the companies installing the new systems straight away, because that work would boom for a year or two. I'd move some of my funds into companies building the robots, and keep a year of spending in cash. I'd move cities if that's where the installation jobs were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be busy, which helps, but under it I'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move cities. What would you be leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not that much, honestly. My mum's an hour away and I'd miss Sunday lunch with her. The cat comes with me. Luka and the lunch arguments, I'd miss those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been upbeat in the other pictures. What's different here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the others I'm ahead of the wave. Here the wave's faster than anyone can paddle. I can still ride it for a bit, but I can see where it breaks.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be a wild couple of years and governments should get support in place fast. Not the end of the world, but not fine either.
S2.think: Two years is too fast even for him: his plan to fix robots fails if robots soon fix themselves. His savings help for a year or two, not forever.
S2.do: Tries to get hired straight away by companies installing new systems and moves some funds into robot-making companies while keeping a year of cash. Moves cities if that's where installation work is.
S2.feel: Anxious underneath, though staying busy helps.
S2.quote: In the others I'm ahead of the wave. Here the wave's faster than anyone can paddle.
S2.fieldNote: His adaptability lets him see a short window of opportunity in installation work, but he's clear-eyed that it closes. He'd hedge by owning part of what replaces him. Leaving town would cost little, mostly Sunday lunch with his mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable if people start now. Learn the new tools, save what you can, and push governments to get support ready. I'd say the people who move first will have more options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to become a technician and do a few years of real automation work. That's enough to build up savings and investments, so when it arrives I'm in a decent spot. I'd still be thirty-two with no job, which is strange to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course this year, get the robot certificate next year and move to an integrator by year two. I'd invest a good chunk of the higher pay, maybe a thousand a month. In year four I'd start thinking about what I'd do after, maybe something with my hands that people pay for because a person did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a plan, but I can see the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Something people pay for because a person did it. What do you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I fix old radios and amplifiers as a hobby, valve ones from the seventies. People pay silly money for one repaired by a human who cares. Maybe that's a small business one day, I don't know if it's enough to live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about anyone else in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, she works in a call centre, and AI would take that faster than my job. She's fifty-five. I'd probably end up helping her out with money, which I'd be happy to do.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight but doable if people start now: learn the tools, save and push for support. Those who move first will have more options.
S3.think: Five years lets him become a technician and do a few years of automation work, building savings and investments. Still, he'd be thirty-two with no job, which feels strange.
S3.do: Finishes the PLC course this year, gets the robot certificate next year and joins an integrator by year two. Invests about a thousand a month and from year four explores repairing vintage radios as a small business.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a plan but the end in view.
S3.quote: People pay silly money for one repaired by a human who cares.
S3.fieldNote: Five years brings him down from anxious to uneasy because he can earn and invest through the boom. His hobby of fixing old valve radios hints at a craft future. His mother's call centre job worries him more than his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare if people take it seriously. Learn, save, and make sure the government has a plan for the end. I'd say I'm optimistic, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine in this one. I'd have ten years of rising pay as a technician, plus investments in the companies doing the automating. By thirty-seven I might have enough to live modestly without a job, and that doesn't scare me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the courses, move to automation work by year two, and invest steadily, maybe more in property later on. I'd build up the radio repair as a side business so it's real by the time AGI lands. I'd help my mum retrain early, maybe pay for a course for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, curious more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said living without a job doesn't scare you much. Why not, when it scares a lot of people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've never been my job. I'm the guy who fixes radios, who visits his mum, who reads about rockets. The job's how I pay for that, so if the job goes and the money's still there, I'm okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your investments don't hold up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair, I've lost money before, so I know they can go down. That's why I'd want the radio business and some property too, so it's not all in one place. And if it all goes wrong, everyone's in the same boat, so I'd hope there's a government plan by then.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people take it seriously: learn, save and make sure government has a plan. He'd call himself optimistic.
S4.think: He thinks he'd be fine, with ten years of rising technician pay and investments in automating companies. By thirty-seven he might live modestly without a job, which doesn't scare him.
S4.do: Moves to automation work by year two and invests steadily, later adding property. Builds his radio repair into a real side business by the time AGI lands and pays for his mother to retrain early.
S4.quote: Because I've never been my job. I'm the guy who fixes radios, who visits his mum, who reads about rockets.
S4.fieldNote: A strong cushion, early investing and a sense of self outside work make him genuinely calm with ten years. He hedges because he remembers losing money before. His main concern shifts to helping his mother.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because nobody can move fast enough, me included. What would help is government support that kicks in quickly, plus free training so people like my mum and Luka get a fair shot, not just people like me who already like this stuff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd want the world to look like after. I'd want people to have time for things like fixing radios, and I'd want it to be normal to say I don't have a job, I fix things for fun. That would be a good outcome, if the money works.

headlineQuote: My whole plan was to be the guy who fixes the robots, and in this one the robots fix themselves pretty quickly.
portrait: Rafael Novak is a 27-year-old junior pick-and-place operator at an electronics plant making circuit boards, studying PLCs in the evenings and using AI every day. He lives alone with his cat, saves frugally and invests in index funds after an early crypto loss. Pragmatic and blame-free, he sees steady change as a chance to become an automation technician. AGI in two years makes him anxious because the robots soon fix themselves, but with five or ten years he plans to ride the installation boom, invest, and grow his vintage radio repair hobby. He says he's never been his job, which keeps him calm in the slowest AGI picture.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because nobody, including him, could adapt fast enough.
whatWouldHelp: Quick government support and free training that gives people like his mother and his colleague Luka a fair chance, not just people who already like technology.
